criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural household access to basic municipal water services (standpipes in yard, piped water inside the house, communal taps, and water cut-offs) and sanitation services (flush toilets and pit latrines), alongside electricity and refuse removal.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, legal and governance instruments (the 1996 Constitution, the Local Government Municipal Systems Act No. 32 of 2000, and the Batho Pele White Paper) are cited only as unanalysed macro-policy background in the Introduction, while the empirical study solely describes physical service levels, technical/physical causes of interruptions (e.g., broken pipes, rusted taps), household coping strategies, and subjective satisfaction ratings with municipal service delivery without empirically examining any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, it clearly fails because it investigates generic municipal service delivery and beneficiary satisfaction rather than any rule-type mechanism directly governing water or sanitation access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure rules, water/sanitation tariffs, discretion, enforcement, or regulatory/ownership structure; electricity subsidy and illegal-connection fines appear only as brief participant recommendations for electricity).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data from a descriptive household survey of 80 rural households in Ward 11 of Lepelle-Nkumpi Local Municipality using a face-to-face semi-structured questionnaire.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports descriptive outcomes directly relevant to household water and sanitation access and continuity, including water source type (Table 2), prevalence of water cut-offs (59%, Section 3.2.2), municipal sanitation access (92%, Section 3.4.1), and toilet typology (Figure 1), in addition to satisfaction ratings.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (80 rural households in Ward 11), outcomes, and descriptive survey design are identifiable, but there is no identifiable legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance exposure variable examined in the univariate survey data.

evidence_quotes.quote: The Local Government Municipal Systems Act No.32 of 2000 requires a municipality to give priority to the basic needs of the local community, promote the development of the local community, and ensure that all members of the local community have access to at least the minimum level of basic municipal services.
A descriptive survey research design was adopted to examine rural households’ satisfaction with access to basic services in Lepelle-Nkumpi municipality.
The above table shows that half of the respondents reported that they have access to standpipes in the yard, followed by the respondents who have access to the communal taps.

The finding indicated that the majority of 74 (92%) of the respondents surveyed indicated that they have access to sanitation services from the municipality, while 6 (8%) of the respondents indicated that they do not have access to sanitation services.

It was assumed that access to basic services does not entirely guarantee satisfaction by the beneficiary households. Hence, this paper focuses on the level of services, quality of services and satisfaction of the rural households.

raw_response.exposure: None (descriptive survey of municipal basic service levels, physical causes of service cut-offs, and household satisfaction; no legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor empirically examined)
raw_response.outcome: Household water source access (standpipes in yard, piped water in dwelling, communal taps), water cut-offs and coping strategies, municipal sanitation access and toilet type (flush toilet, pit latrine with/without ventilation), and satisfaction ratings with municipal service provision
raw_response.population_and_sample: Rural households residing in Ward 11, Lepelle-Nkumpi Local Municipality, Capricorn District, Limpopo Province, South Africa (target population N = 2,300 households; surveyed sample n = 80 households)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although this empirical household survey (n = 80) measures rural household water and sanitation access, water cut-offs, coping strategies, and satisfaction in Lepelle-Nkumpi Local Municipality, South Africa, it does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance mechanism governing water or sanitation access (nor any empirical governance exposure under the plain reading of Criterion 2). Statutory mandates appear only as unanalysed background in the Introduction, while the empirical analysis reports univariate frequencies of service levels, physical infrastructure breakdowns (broken pipes, old taps), and beneficiary satisfaction with generic municipal service delivery.
raw_response.study_design: Descriptive cross-sectional household survey using a face-to-face semi-structured questionnaire (described as convenience sampling of 80 households in Methodology and random selection in Abstract)
